title: Yampa Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Yampa wells have a 62-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock and depths up to 2,536 feet can change drilling costs.
h1: What Yampa Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land near Yampa means dealing with mountain-bedrock wells, not a uniform underground water system. Records within five miles show 145 permitted wells, with 89 recorded as constructed. Of those, 88 report a total depth, so the depth data is useful but not complete.

The local record points to generally shallow wells and solid reported yields, with important exceptions. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. That makes nearby well records valuable, but it does not guarantee the same result on your parcel. Use this information to set expectations, compare drilling bids, and investigate water, septic, access, and building constraints before closing.

sections.heading: Yampa Well Depths Range From Shallow to Very Deep
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Yampa is 62 feet. The middle half runs from 35 to 122 feet, which means many local drilling projects are relatively shallow. The depth mix supports that pattern: 64% of wells are under 100 feet, while 24% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

There is still substantial variation. The 90th percentile is 364 feet, and the deepest record reaches 2,536 feet. In mountain fractured rock, a nearby shallow well does not prove your lot will be shallow. A driller should review neighboring logs, geology, access, casing, and grout requirements before giving a firm bid.

sections.heading: Most Yampa Wells Report Useful Production
sections.html:
Only 26 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the production sample is limited. Among those reports, the median yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 6.0 and 11.8 gallons per minute. That is a workable range for many household uses, but a yield test is still necessary for a specific property.

No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. Another 19% produce between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 62% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 19% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Ask for the well-construction report and pumping information, not just a verbal production claim.

sections.heading: Yampa Water Levels Look Shallow in the Available Records
sections.html:
Only 6 wells report a static water level, so this is a small sample rather than a basinwide measurement. The median depth to water is 9 feet, and the middle half is 4 to 16 feet. Those readings indicate shallow static water levels in the reported wells.

The permit history does not provide a complete, consistent water-level series by decade, so it cannot establish that the water table is rising or dropping near Yampa. A static level is also not the same as a dependable pumping rate. Have the well tested after construction, and ask how the measurement was taken. Seasonal conditions, nearby pumping, and fractured rock can make one reading a poor predictor of long-term performance.

sections.heading: Yampa Permit History Shows Most Activity After the Early Years
sections.html:
Permit records show the strongest period of activity in the 1990s, with 49 permits. The record includes 15 permits in the 1970s, 15 in the 1980s, 24 in the 2000s, 11 in the 2010s, and 8 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2023.

The most frequently listed drillers are Arrow Drilling (Berglund, Peter R.), Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Joe Wayne), and Interstate Water Wells, Inc. (Kuchler, Leroy E.). These names describe permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, availability, casing and grout specifications, testing, and who handles the DWR paperwork.

sections.heading: A Typical Yampa Well Can Cost More Than the Hole Alone
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. Drilling is modeled at $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 62 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $4,000 to $6,200.

That is not the complete water system. A finished well with a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $10,000 to $18,200. A bid can move outside that range if the hole must go substantially deeper, access is difficult, casing or grouting changes, or the site needs additional electrical and trench work. Get a written scope that separates drilling, completion, pump equipment, testing, and site restoration.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality, Septic Space, and Mountain-Site Risks
sections.html:
Permit records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 139 wells. They name alluvial aquifers for 2 wells and the Morrison aquifer for 1 well. No wells in the data are identified in a Denver Basin aquifer. Fractured bedrock can produce water through narrow zones, so dry holes and sharp differences between neighboring wells remain possible.

Within about ten miles, mapped environmental records include 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 6 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These listings do not prove contamination at your property. Test the well for appropriate local concerns, review land-use history, and locate septic setbacks, replacement-area needs, driveway grades, and building envelopes before buying.

sections.heading: How to Approach a Yampa Lot Purchase or New Build
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit file for the parcel and nearby wells in Yampa, Phippsburg, and Oak Creek. Compare reported depths, construction details, static levels, and yields, while remembering that only 26 wells report pump yield. The nearby record can narrow expectations, but it cannot promise a result on untested ground.

For an existing home, inspect the pump, pressure system, storage, electrical supply, water quality, and recent production test. For vacant land, obtain a driller’s access review and a written estimate before relying on the 62-foot median. Also confirm the legal water use, septic approval path, and building location. Household-use wells may be exempt wells, but Colorado water-right and augmentation requirements can still matter in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Yampa, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Yampa is 62 feet. The middle half runs from 35 to 122 feet, and 64% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Depths vary sharply in fractured mountain bedrock, however: the 90th percentile is 364 feet and the deepest record is 2,536 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Yampa?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 62-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $4,000 to $6,200. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,000 to $18,200. A deeper hole or difficult access can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Yampa wells produce?
faq.a: Only 26 wells report pump yield, so the sample is limited. The median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 6.0 to 11.8 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, but a buyer should require a property-specific pump test and review the construction report.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Yampa?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that water is safe to drink. Test the individual well. Within about ten miles are 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 6 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those mapped locations do not prove a problem at your lot, but they support reviewing land history and testing for appropriate contaminants.

Many are. The median reported depth is 62 feet, 64% are under 100 feet, and the middle half is 35 to 122 feet. Still, Yampa wells are commonly associated with fractured-bedrock conditions, and the record includes wells as deep as 2,536 feet. Nearby depth is useful for planning, not a guarantee for a new well.
